newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIAN PARLIAMENT BACKS GOVERNMENT IN VOTE.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIAN PARLIAMENT BACKS GOVERNMENT IN VOTE.

text.p: Romania's parliament endorsed the centrist government's proposed fast-track reforms on Friday by easily defeating a confidence vote called by the ex-communist opposition thrown out of office last year.

Members voted after a 12-hour debate 277 to 158 to throw out the first of two motions accusing the government of failing to keep election promises to improve living standards, cut taxes and help industry and agriculture. A second motion is to be considered next week.

Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, speaking before the vote, said his programme had restored Romania's economic credibility, badly battered during the seven years leftists held power following the execution of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
"We have managed to win credibility and attract foreign investors to revive the economy," he said. "We must continue our reform programme to keep from disappointing the people."

Ciorbea said prolonged mismanagement by the ex-communists had pitched the country into crisis. His government was now taming inflation, stabilising the leu currency and preparing Romania for integration with the European Union.
"The current situation is the legacy of the former government," he said.

"Industrial policy in recent years was a failure. We will support only those sectors which can compete with our future EU partners. It is not the government which is closing down factories. They are being closed down by market laws."
The opposition acknowledged that Ciorbea's programme had widespread support but warned that austerity measures had pushed the country close to breaking point.
"For the first time we have layoffs in the private sector, which has come under pressure from tax policies," he said.

"You enjoy great popular support and foreign support, you have a market infrastructure set up by the former government. Don't miss the opportunities to develop Romania. These opportunities are on the brink of being lost."
President Emil Constantinescu and his government pledge to press ahead with reforms which have cut average monthly salaries in recent months to the equivalent of less than $80.
International lenders have praised their efforts, with the International Monetary Fund extending credits of $430 million and the World Bank offering a further $550 million in loans.

Opinion polls show most Romanians support reforms despite a widening gap in living standards with other ex-communist countries like Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. Trade unions have mounted only minor protests so far.

Many commentators have said the opposition motion amounts to little more than an attempt to divert attention from its own serious divisions. The main opposition Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), headed by former president Ion Iliescu, is riven by a revolt by a faction demanding leadership changes.
